title: The share of studies with a positive effect is overstated, in two places
published:
Across the 67 studies we summarize, [[three-fourths]] find a positive effect of being described as a woman.

We observe considerable study-to-study variation, although [[more than three-fourths]] of the studies show a positive effect.
corrected:
Across the 67 studies we summarize, [[70%]] find a positive effect of being described as a woman.

We observe considerable study-to-study variation, although [[70%]] of the studies show a positive effect.
note: Of the 67 study-level estimates, 47 are positive, 19 are negative and 1 is exactly zero. The positive share is 70.1 per cent, which is below three-fourths rather than above it. The claim the two sentences make is unaffected: positive effects are the large majority.

title: The counts of negative and of significant estimates
published: We see a very consistent pattern in favor of women candidates on average: 47 estimates are positive ([[23]] significant) and [[18]] are negative ([[11]] significant).
corrected: We see a very consistent pattern in favor of women candidates on average: 47 estimates are positive ([[29]] significant) and [[19]] are negative ([[6]] significant).
note:
The deposited estimates divide into 47 positive, 19 negative and 1 exactly zero, which is the only division summing to 67. The published 47 plus 18 sums to 65.

The corrected counts of significant estimates are those of the confidence interval rule the deposited script itself applies, which gives 29 and 6. The published 23 and 11 correspond to no significance rule the deposited estimates support, and not merely to a rule with a different threshold: both counts rise as a threshold is relaxed, so no threshold can produce 23 and 11 at once. Tightening the threshold until only 23 positive estimates remain significant leaves 5 negative ones; loosening it until 11 negative estimates are significant leaves 43 positive ones. A test of p below 0.05 gives 19 and 2, and cannot be what was done in any case, because 19 of the 67 studies carry no p-value. What procedure produced the published pair is therefore unknown; the correction states what the deposited rule gives.

The direction of the correction favours the article's own claim: more positive estimates reach significance than were reported, and fewer negative ones.

A count of significant estimates is the warrant for the sentences that follow it, so those were re-asked under the corrected rule. The article asserts a significance verdict for three studies one at a time, all on published p. 661, and all three keep the verdict it gives them: Ono and Yamada is negative and significant, Kage, Rosenbluth, and Tanaka is positive and significant, and Horiuchi, Smith, and Yamamoto is exactly zero. The same paragraph names five further contexts as showing negative effects and claims significance for none of them, and the deposit gives a negative estimate in every one. No sentence in the article changes.

title: Figure 3 covers 37 experiments, not 36
published: Figure 3 shows the CATEs of candidate gender, conditional on respondent gender, for the [[36]] experiments where we were able to identify respondent gender.
corrected: Figure 3 shows the CATEs of candidate gender, conditional on respondent gender, for the [[37]] experiments where we were able to identify respondent gender.
note: The deposited respondent-gender file carries 37 studies, and the published figure itself draws 37 rows in each of its two panels. Figure 3 is correct as printed and is not reproduced here; only the sentence describing it miscounts. Nothing plotted is affected and neither pooled estimate moves.

title: Appendix Table A.1 omits one of the studies it summarizes
note:
The appendix carries 44 per-study CATE figures, A.2 through A.45, one for each study in the meta-analysis. Simas and Murdoch (2019) is plotted at Figure A.44 and has no row in Table A.1, so the table describes 43 of the 44. The study is present in the deposited data and in every pooled estimate; only the summary table omits it.

The omission is not confined to the table. The appendix introduces Figure A.1 as the distribution of the CATEs "conditional on each of the attributes listed in Table A.1", so the table is where a reader learns what that figure covers, and the unlisted study contributes 2 of the figure's 954 conditional effects. Two estimates in 954 cannot move the distribution, so the appendix's takeaway from Figure A.1 stands as written. What the missing row costs is the account of one study's attributes, which is the whole of what Table A.1 exists to give.

title: The Clayton and Nyhan (2020) manuscript has six authors
published: [[Clayton, Katherine, and Brendan Nyhan]]. 2020. "Who Will Defend Democracy?  Evaluating Tradeoffs in Candidate Support among Partisan Donors and Voters."  Unpublished manuscript.
corrected: Carey, John, Katherine Clayton, Gretchen Helmke, Brendan Nyhan, Mitchell Sanders, and  Susan Stokes. 2020. "Who Will Defend Democracy? Evaluating Tradeoffs in Candidate  Support among Partisan Donors and Voters." Unpublished manuscript.
note: The manuscript at the URL the entry itself prints carries six authors on its title page, in the alphabetical order given above. Crossref, doi 10.33774/apsa-2019-wjva3-v4: Nyhan, Helmke, Sanders, Clayton, Carey, Stokes, and the same six on every posted version of the preprint. The short form is therefore Carey et al. (2020), which the article uses as a study label in six further places: two rows of Table 1, two rows of the appendix's study table, and the titles of appendix Figures A.16 and A.17. The appendix's own reference list carries the same two-author entry. Only the labels change: no estimate, standard error, sample size or study is affected, and neither of the two experiments the label names is misidentified.

title: An appendix reference prints a URL cut off at the edge of the page
note: The line the appendix sets this URL on runs 206pt past the right edge of the paper, so 23 characters of it are drawn where no reader can see them and the printed URL leads nowhere. Two independent records give the same missing span: the authors' own gender.bib in the archived working folder, and the ARTICLE'S OWN reference list on published p. 666, which prints the whole URL because its two-column measure broke the line somewhere else. Nothing but the URL changes: the entry names the same manuscript, which is the one entry 6 corrects the authorship of.

title: An appendix reference prints a URL with a character missing
note: The tilde is drawn as a blank: the published page shows a gap at 300 dpi and the text layer returns a space, so the character is absent from the document rather than lost in reading it. Without it the URL is not a personal-directory URL and does not resolve. The authors' own gender.bib in the archived working folder carries the tilde. The article's reference list cites a different address for the same manuscript and so cannot settle this one.

title: A plural noun where the sentence wants a modifier
published: Finally, we consider the effects of gender, conditional on respondent characteristics, in particular by gender and [[partisans]] affiliations.
corrected: Finally, we consider the effects of gender, conditional on respondent characteristics, in particular by gender and [[partisan]] affiliations.
note: The error is the authors' own and survived a copy-edit that touched the same sentence: the submitted manuscript in the archived working folder carries the same words but opens them "Lastly" where the page prints "Finally". The same paper writes "candidate partisan affiliation" correctly on published p. 657. One letter changes and nothing else does: no estimate, count, figure or study is affected, and the sentence means what a reader already takes it to mean.
